articles.text: The most scurrilous libel that even long-suffering Medora has ever endured, is contained in the following Bismarck telegram to a Chicago paper, dated April 16: "At Medora last evening, (1) the cowboys of the Bad Lands (2) indulged in a dance at a leading hotel and although no one was killed, the event was worthy of notice.(3) The Marquis de Mores, having returned from the east, has started operations at his Medora ranch(4) and the cowboys were rejoicing over their source of financial supply.(5) The hotel was filled with transients,(6) most of whom were called to the place by business relationships with the Marquis.(7) The dance was at its height at midnight. The female population of the Bad Lands was present and the cowboys were determined to show their mettle and worth.(8) At midnight, revolvers were drawn(9) and from that time until morning,(10) the fusillade drowned the music of the orchestra.(11) Every bed-room in the hotel was shot into(12) and that no one was killed, is looked upon as a miracle.(13) Dr. Williamson of this city, occupied a room near the ball-room(14) and his door was perforated(15) so that it resembled the lid of a pepper-box.(16) In the morning, he picked up numerous bullets in his room, (17)—enough, according to one story, to fill a quart cup(18)—and he believes that his life was saved by the mattress, under which he remained during the night.(19) Every guest was paralyzed with fear(20) and from the number of bullets shot into their rooms(21) all feel grateful that they escaped with their lives.(22) Not once during the night did the dancing cease,(23) women and men cheering and yelling,(24) as each volley was fired.(25)" Whether the author of the above was actuated by malice or a craving for the sensational, it is hard to decide. Certain it is that there are in the above article, twenty-five separate and distinct lies. It might be best to show them by mentioning the exact facts. The ball was held on the evening of April 12, and was managed by Fred A. Willard and Moses Ryder, sufficient guarantee, if there had been any need of it, that there would be no disturbance whatever. The dance was not given in honor of the opening up of any new work here, for the season's work has not as yet opened up in any of its branches, but was given in honor of the stockmen who were present for the purpose of attending the election and the stockgrowers' meeting. The dance was attended by the stockmen and citizens, with their wives and daughters and the low-minded flings at the "female population of the Bad Lands" who were "cheering and yelling as each volley was fired" are enough to make the blood of every man who knows the facts, boil with indignation. Nowhere can be found truer or more perfect women than are found right here in the Bad Lands. To intimate that they would in any way approve of such a ruffianly trait as the discharging of a revolver inside of a house, or any "bad man" shooting outside, is an insult hard to be borne by the husbands and fathers in the Bad Lands. There was one shot and one only, fired in the hotel that night and for that matter, the only one that has been discharged there since Mr. Boyd assumed the management. This one was fired by some drunken tenderfoot in the hall in front of Dr. Williamson's room, which by the way, was the farthest removed in the hotel from the dining-room, which was used for dancing. Although no one at the dance was in the slightest degree intoxicated, we say that this man was drunk because he made considerable noise in the halls by colliding with Dr. Williamson's door, before discharging his revolver. That the man was a tenderfoot is shown by the fact that his was a 38-calibre revolver, which made so little noise that only a few who were in the office of the hotel, heard the discharge and after discussing its probable whereabouts, concluded that it was fired near the depot. From extensive inquiry, we are satisfied that this was the only shot fired in Medora during the evening. The bullet went through the plastering in the hall and rebounded from the brick to the floor, where it was picked up in the morning by Dr. Williamson on coming out of his room. Not a shot that or any other night, ever went through a door in the hotel. If the Bismarck perjurer will come here and show us a solitary hole shot through Dr. Williamson's or any other guest's door, we will fill it with diamonds and give to him in token of the clearness and beauty of that truth which he so rarely stumbles upon. The most of the blame for this criminal libel on Medora is now laid to Dr. Williamson, who undoubtedly took a highly colored account of the affair to Bismarck. We think we can put our finger on the man who sent the telegram to Chicago and who will probably be called on in a suit for libel to explain his version of the matter. Our columns are open to Dr. Williamson to vindicate himself from connection with what he knows to be an entirely unjust commentary on Medora, a slander on the citizens of the Bad Lands and an insult to every woman here.
articles.summary: Packard quotes and rebuts, point by point, a Bismarck telegram to a Chicago paper describing an all-night shooting spree at a Medora hotel dance; he says the April 12 ball was orderly, only one shot was fired by a drunken tenderfoot, and blames Dr. Williamson for the exaggerated account.

articles.text: There is no disguising the fact that there was some foundation, though ever so slight, for the above article, in the discharging of a revolver. Sheriff Willard is in earnest in the article published in this issue, stating that the law in respect to the discharge of fire-arms will be strictly enforced, and we look for the practice to fall into "innocnous desuetude."
articles.summary: Packard notes that Sheriff Willard means to enforce the law against discharging fire-arms.

articles.headline: Range Bulls.
articles.text:
Parties in want of yearling Shorthorn or Durham bulls will do well to correspond with W. A. VanBrunt of Horicon, Wisconsin.

The calves were purchased last spring on account of their high breeding and the specific merits of their parents. They have been wintered with the especial view of putting on the range this spring.
articles.summary: Notice that W. A. VanBrunt of Horicon, Wisconsin, has yearling Shorthorn or Durham bulls for range use.

articles.summary: Stock Inspector Willard advertises an estray roan horse taken up about Dec. 1, 1885.

articles.text:
District No. 6.

Commences at Medora, D. T., May 25, 1886; works down Little Missouri to the mouth of Big Beaver creek; thence up Big Beaver creek to its head; thence across to the Little Beaver at the crossing of the old government road; thence down Little Beaver to its mouth; thence across to northern Hashknife camp on Little Missouri and down to Medora. John Goodall, foreman.

District No. 7.

Commences June 1, 1886, at the mouth of Big Beaver: works up said stream in conjunction with round-up No. 6 to the head of Big Beaver; thence across to the heads of Glendive and Cedar creeks and down said creeks to the Yellowstone; thence working down the south side of the Yellowstone and tributaries to Fort Buford. S. H. Tarbell, foreman.
articles.summary: Routes, dates and foremen for spring round-up districts No. 6 (from Medora, May 25) and No. 7 (from the mouth of Big Beaver, June 1).

articles.text: The weekly St. Paul Pioneer Press of April 1, speaks very highly of the Shorthorn cattle from the Mayville Farm, Mayville, Traill Co., Dak., to be offered at Public Sale on the Old Fair Grounds, Minneapolis, Minnesota, May 26, 1886. It says, "The proprietors, J. L. & E. B. Grandin, started their herd seven years ago and spared no expense to procure animals of choice breeding from such celebrated families as Peri, Rosamond, Princess, Rosaballa, Goodness, Victoria, Sutherland, Kirklemington, and others. This is a good opportnnity for stockmen and farmers to avail themselves of this sale and improve their stock." Catalogue sent on application to the farm. H. F. Brown of Minneapolis, will also sell about thirty head of Short Horn cattle, May 25, and Lieut. Governor C. A. Gilman and N. P. Clark of St. Cloud, Minnesota, will sell forty-five head of Short Horn cattle, May 27. Both on the Old Fair Grounds, Minneapolis, Minnesota.
articles.summary: Notice of Shorthorn cattle sales at Minneapolis, May 25-27, 1886, including the Grandins' Mayville Farm herd.

articles.headline: Notice.
articles.text:
Notice is hereby given that section 495 of the Penal Code, will be strictly enforced on and after this date, May 5, 1886. The section reads as follows: "Every person who willfully discharges any species of fire-arms, air-gun or other weapon, or throws any other missile in any public place, where there is any person to be endangered thereby, although no injury to any person shall ensue, is guilty of a misdemeanor.

Fred. A. Willard,
Sheriff.
articles.summary: Sheriff Willard gives notice that the penal code section against discharging fire-arms in public places will be strictly enforced from May 5, 1886.

articles.headline: Additional Local.
articles.text: T. W. Gordon wishes us to announce that the sale advertised in this issue is a genuine one and that it will afford an unprecedented opportunity to buy cheap goods.
articles.summary: T. W. Gordon's advertised sale is said to be genuine.

articles.text: George Frazer and Riley Brooks left this morning for the Hashknife camp, where they will represent the Ref. Car Co. in the round-up which starts from there about the 17th.
articles.summary: Frazer and Brooks leave to represent the Refrigerator Car Co. at the round-up starting from the Hashknife camp about the 17th.

articles.text: The Marquis is now in Milwaukee, making arrangements with the brewers to supply them with malt and to receive from them the refuse, which is the basis of the new fattening food, called "brewers' grain."
articles.summary: The Marquis de Morès is in Milwaukee arranging to trade malt for brewers' grain as cattle feed.

articles.text: The Commissioners' ideas of the way to run the county, cannot be too highly praised, and bid fair to be carried out to the letter. In brief, they propose that the same rules shall guide them as do in the conduct of any business.
articles.summary: Praise for the new county commissioners' businesslike approach.

articles.text: The citizens of St. Paul are entertaining the committee sent there to discuss the matter of establishing stock-yards, to make a market for western cattle. This committee will stop at Medora on its return, to look over the plans of the Marquis for establishing a fattery here. They were to arrive to-night, but it is doubtful if they will be here before Sunday.
articles.summary: A committee discussing St. Paul stock-yards will stop at Medora to look over the Marquis's plans for a fattery.

articles.text: Wm. Benson of Dickinson, day before yesterday shot a very large silver-tip bear, on Knife river.
articles.summary: Wm. Benson of Dickinson shot a large silver-tip bear on Knife river.

articles.text: A letter from Charlie Galligan, foreman for the Hashknife outfit, states that that company will drive 40,000 head of cattle to their northern range this summer. They will come in thirteen herds. He also states that there was considerable unexpected loss among the cattle during March.
articles.summary: The Hashknife outfit will drive 40,000 cattle north in thirteen herds this summer, after unexpected March losses.

articles.text: The inaugural address of Chairman of the Board Truscott is too good to be lost. It ran as follows: "Mr. McKenzie proposed me for chairman and I proposed Mr. McKenzie. Whereupon we compromised on me. I therefore declare myself duly elected and call the board to order."
articles.summary: Humorous report of J. L. Truscott's 'inaugural address' as chairman of the county board.

articles.text: Willis Eaton will probably begin assessing on Saturday of this week. Under the new rules by which everything is to be assessed at its full value, and the railroad tax of over $5,000, we confidently expect that the rate will be under six mills. If so, we will have the lowest rate of any county in Dakota.
articles.summary: Assessor Willis Eaton to begin assessing Saturday; the paper expects a county tax rate under six mills.

articles.text: Lloyd Roberts went through Medora to Glendive, Sunday morning, where he delivered several cars of cattle to Mr. Bangs. He returned Monday and left this morning again for St. Cloud, where he has contracted for more cattle. His daughter Lizzie went with him, to attend school in Minnesota.
articles.summary: Lloyd Roberts delivered cattle at Glendive and left for St. Cloud with his daughter Lizzie, who will attend school in Minnesota.

articles.text: A cousin of J. A. VanEeghen is now visiting at the VE ranch. The last word received from VanEeghen was that horses were scarcer in Washington Ter. than he expected, but that he was making fair progress. He expects to buy at least four hundred mares and more, if he can buy them right. He has not yet decided whether to drive or ship.
articles.summary: A cousin of J. A. VanEeghen is visiting the VE ranch while VanEeghen buys mares in Washington Territory.

articles.text: We have an over-stock of 3½ Studebaker wagons that the Studebaker M'f'g. Co. have instructed us to close out at $75 each. These wagons have never turned a wheel under a load, are new and first-class in every respect, have the Co's. full guarantee for 5,000 pounds, according to old freighters are the best ironed and easiest running wagon of its size in the world, and cost at the factory, $87 each in car lots. There never has been and never will be again such a bargain in wagons in this country. The $75 rate is cash of course and holds good for one or more. For further particulars, call at or address the Cow Boy office.
articles.summary: Packard offers surplus 3½ Studebaker wagons at $75 each.

articles.headline: Commissioners' Meeting.
articles.text:
Minutes of a [special?] meeting of the Board of County Commissioners (elect,) held at the office of D. McKenzie, on the fourth day of May, 1886.

Present: Commissioners Truscott and McKenzie and Clerk Williamson.

The board, after having first taken the oath of office, proceeded to elect a chairman.

It was moved and seconded that J. L. Truscott act as chairman. Carried.

On motion of J. L. Truscott, a resolution fixing the amounts of the bonds of the various county officers (elect) was adopted as follows:
County Treasurer, $4,000,
Justices of Peace, $300,
Constables, $200,
Register and Ex. Co. Clerk, $1,000,
Judge of Probate, $2,000,
Sheriff, $3,000,
Coroner, $1,000,
Assessor, $2,000.

On motion of McKenzie, the board adjourned to meet at 7 o'clock on the morning of May 5.

J. C. Williamson,
Co. Clerk.

Meeting on Morning of May 5.

Present: Commissioners Truscott and McKenzie and Clerk Williamson.

Meeting called to order by Chairman Truscott.

The reading of the minutes of the preceding meeting was omitted.

Bids for the county books from the Pioneer Press and Geo. D. Barnard & Co. were opened and it being found that the latter's bid was the lowest at $386.50, it was accepted.

On motion, the board adjourned to meet at one o'clock.

J. C. Williamson,
Co. Clerk.

Meeting on Afternoon of May 5.

Meeting was called to order by the chairman.

Present: McKenzie, Truscott and Clerk Williamson.

Fred. A. Willard's bond as sheriff came before the board and was accepted. Sureties: M. Wadsworth and Wm. F. VanDriesche.

The County clerk was ordered by the board to procure letter-heads of The Bad Lands Cow Boy.

On motion of McKenzie, the board adjourned to meet at seven o'clock in the evening.

J. C. Williamson,
Co. Clerk.

Meeting on Evening of May 5.

Meeting called to order by Chairman Truscott.

Present: Commissioners Truscott and McKenzie and Clerk Willamson.

The first business was the examination of the bonds of the Register, Coroner and Justices Copeland and Elmer.

On motion of McKenzie, the bonds were accepted.

An extra order of official supplies to the amount of $80.80, of Geo. D. Barnard & Co., St. Louis, Mo., was made.

On motion of McKenzie, the Board adjourned, to meet the second Thursday in May.

J. C. Williamson,
Co. Clerk.
articles.summary: Minutes of the first meetings of the Billings County commissioners (elect), May 4-5, 1886: Truscott elected chairman, officers' bonds fixed and accepted, county books ordered.

articles.text: J. H. Gordon and wife and Joseph Hanauer of Glendive, were here Sunday, on a visit to T. W. Gordon.
articles.summary: J. H. Gordon, his wife and Joseph Hanauer of Glendive visited T. W. Gordon on Sunday.

articles.text: Dr. Stickney of Dickinson, was here last Saturday. Hereafter, he will be in Medora twice a week. The Dr. is now the railroad surgeon, taking the place of Dr. Robarts, who now has charge of Hunter's Hot Springs.
articles.summary: Dr. Stickney of Dickinson, the new railroad surgeon replacing Dr. Robarts, will visit Medora twice a week.

articles.text: To-day's showers are a perfect god-send to the stockmen. Although the grass was well started a week or ten days ago, it has grown but little, if any, since that time. It will now get a good permanent start.
articles.summary: Rain showers on the issue day help the stalled range grass.

articles.text: It will make Assessor Eaton rustle hard to get through his work by July 1. He must, according to law, assess from Cave Hills on the south, to the Missouri river on the north and to Stark county on the east, making a territory in round numbers 200x50 miles. Our assessor's cowboy training will stand him in good stead.
articles.summary: Assessor Eaton must assess a territory of about 200 by 50 miles by July 1.

articles.text: Charles Eaton and bride returned Monday evening from their bridal trip, being accompanied by Mrs. Eaton's mother. The party is now visiting at the Logging Camp, before going home to the SOHO ranch. Mrs. Eaton and mother are warmly welcomed to the Bad Lands, which is to be their future home. They are both accomplished musicians and we look for many a happy social gathering at the SOHO ranch.
articles.summary: Charles Eaton and his bride, with her mother, returned from their wedding trip and are visiting the Logging Camp before settling at the SOHO ranch.

articles.headline: Sheriff's Sale.
articles.text:
Ter. of Dakota, County of Morton, To which county Billings county is attached for judicial purposes. } ss.

Notice is hereby given that by virtue of a judgment and decree in foreclosure, rendered and given by the District Court of the sixth judicial district, in and for the county of Morton, (to which county Billings county is attached for judicial purposes,) and Territory of Dakota, and filed in the office of said court, on the 23rd. day of April, A. D. 1886, in an action wherein the Northern Pacific Refrigerator Car Company is plaintiff and John Kiefer and Mary J. Kiefer are defendants, in favor of said plaintiff, and against said defendant, for the sum of One thousand three hundred and twenty-seven dollars and fifty-three cents ($1,327.53,) the principal and interest secured by a certain mortgage, given by John Kiefer and Mary J. Kiefer, his wife, to the Northern Pacific Refrigerator Car Company, together with interest thereon from April 10th., A. D. 1886, the date of said decree and also the cost of said plaintiff, taxed at the sum of ninety-one dollars and thirty-five cents, ($91.35,) which judgment and decree directed the sale by me of the real estate hereinafter described, to satisfy the amount of said judgment, with interest thereon, and costs and expenses of said sale, or so much thereof as the proceeds of such sale, applicable thereto, will satisfy, and by virtue of a writ issued out of the office of the Clerk of said court, in and for said county of Morton, to which county, Billings county is attached for judicial purposes, and under the seal of said court, directing me to sell said real property, pursuant to said judgment and decree,

I, George W. Harmon, Sheriff of said Morton county and the person appointed by said court to make said sale, will sell the hereinafter described real estate to the highest bidder, for cash, at public auction, at the front door of the Court House in the city of Mandan, in the county of Morton, (to which county Billings county is attached for judicial purposes,) and Territory of Dakota, on the 17th day of June, A. D. 1886, at two o'clock, P. M., of that day, to satisfy said judgment, interest and costs, and the costs and expenses of such sale, or so much thereof as the proceeds of such sale, applicable thereto, will satisfy.

The premises to be sold as aforesaid, pursuant to said judgment and decree, and to said writ, and to this notice, are described in said judgment, decree and writ, as follows, to-wit:

All those tracts or parcels of land lying and being in the County of Billings, and Territory of Dakota, described as follows:

Lots number Thirteen (13) and Fourteen (14) in Block number nine (9,) as laid down and designated on the plat of the town of Medora, Billings county, D. T., as the same is recorded in the office of Register of Deeds of Morton county, D. T., to which County Billings county, which is unorganized, is attached for judicial purposes.

Dated at Mandan, Dakota. April 29, A. D., 1886.
George W. Harmon, Sheriff,
Morton County, Dakota.
Edward S. Allen, Plaintiff's Att'y.
articles.summary: Foreclosure sale notice: Medora lots 13 and 14, block 9, mortgaged by John and Mary J. Kiefer to the Northern Pacific Refrigerator Car Company, to be sold at Mandan on June 17, 1886.
